name: Software-defined vehicles
summary: Vehicle functions are increasingly controlled by updateable software running on consolidated computing platforms.
useCase: A manufacturer repairs a software fault remotely, updates the user interface and adds a supported function over the vehicle’s life.
whyNow: Automakers are rebuilding electrical architectures and software supply chains. QNX’s large embedded base indicates a foundation for this shift, but an operating system inside a car does not by itself make the car fully software-defined.

mainstream.scope: New vehicle platforms from major manufacturers with centralised computing, managed software updates and ongoing feature maintenance.
mainstream.rationale: Existing software suppliers and announced next-generation platforms support routine use this decade. Vehicle programme cycles slow deployment; the installed vehicle fleet will take much longer to turn over.

metric.name: QNX embedded vehicle installed base
metric.scope: BlackBerry QNX software in vehicles on the road; foundational software proxy
metric.limitations: Cumulative embedded software base, not a count of fully software-defined vehicles or annual new-vehicle sales. Many older systems have limited updateability. No 2026 incremental total is invented.
metric.futureNote: No defensible like-for-like external forecast is available for this KPI. The forward maturity path is a separately labelled analyst scenario, not a numerical adoption forecast.

No comparable 2022 installed-base observation is included in this review.

BlackBerry reported a 275-million-vehicle QNX installed base in its December release.
QNX announced that BMW’s next-generation vehicle platforms would use its technology; current filings still reference 275 million vehicles.

tailwinds: Common software platforms can reduce duplicated engineering
Remote fixes lower some service costs
Vehicle computing suppliers benefit as manufacturers consolidate controllers
bottlenecks: Functional safety and cybersecurity must survive frequent updates
Legacy architectures and supplier contracts complicate migration
Customers may reject paid features or poorly supported software
watchMetrics: Share of new platforms with centralised compute and OTA update coverage
Software-defect recall costs and successful update rates
Per-vehicle software backlog and recurring revenue with clear definitions

forwardInterpretation: The maturity path is an analyst scenario for the stated market scope. A score of 4 means routine use in that scope, not a measured adoption percentage. The window can shift if the listed cost, performance, evidence or policy bottlenecks fail to clear.
